newsitem.title: USA: Medical journal- U.S. marijuana policy inhumane.
newsitem.headline: Medical journal- U.S. marijuana policy inhumane.

text.p: The editor of the New England Journal of Medicine sharply criticised the federal government's threat to prosecute doctors who prescribe marijuana for serious medical problems.
In an editorial in Thursday's issue, Dr. Jerome P. Kassirer wrote that the policy "misguided, heavy-handed and inhumane."

He said doctors who challenge the government's decision will "force the courts to adjudicate between the rights of those at death's door and the absolute power of bureaucrats whose decisions are based more on reflexive ideology and political correctness than on compassion."

Kassirer said although federal officials can be concerned about the long-term effects of marijuana and whether the drug leads to other serious addictions, "neither long-term side effects nor addication is a relevant issue" for seriously ill patients.
"It is also hypocritical to forbid physicians to prescribe marijuana while permitting them to use morphine and meperidine to relieve extreme dyspnea (labored breathing) and pain," he said.
Both are addictive and either drug can hasten death if a little too much is given. "By contrast, there is no risk of death from smoking marijuana," Kassirer said.

He said the federal government should change marijuana's status from Schedule 1, which is for addictive drugs with no medical use, to Schedule 2, where addictive drugs with a legitimate medical use are listed.
If the government supplied the marijuana for Schedule 2 uses, the editor said, it would not be a signal to the young that marijuana is okay for general use.
Meanwhile, the office of federal antidrug chief Barry McCaffrey released a statement on Wednesday disagreeing with Kassirer's position.

"Just as air traffic control and food safety must be approved by experts, medicines must also be determined both safe and effective under established procedures. Selective use of anecdotal data does not make the scientific case," the statement read in part.
McCaffrey said his office has committed $1 million to the Institute of Medicine of the National Academy of Sciences to evaluate all studies conducted to date on marijuana as medicine.
